prompt: In the opening story, two roommates each wrote about their futures in the year {{1}}. By {{2}} the second had achieved all three of his written targets while the first was still writing the same sentence.
explanation: The lecture opens in 2008 and checks back in 2012, four years later.

prompt: What did the lecture say made the difference between the two roommates?

options.text: Clarity
Intelligence
Family background
Luck

explanation: The slide rules out intelligence, family background and luck by name, and settles on clarity.

prompt: Which factors does the lecture explicitly rule out as the reason for the difference? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Intelligence
Family background
Clarity
Luck

explanation: Intelligence, family background and luck are ruled out; clarity is what remained.

prompt: "The indispensable first step to getting what you want is this: decide what you {{1}}." This quotation is credited to Ben {{2}}.
explanation: Ben Stein: decide what you want. It is the opening quotation of Lecture One.

prompt: What did the second roommate actually write down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A certification
An NGO role
A first class degree
500,000 naira saved by a specific date

explanation: The three written targets were a certification, an NGO role and 500,000 naira saved, all by a specific date.

prompt: Which are among the four stated learning objectives of Lecture One? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Distinguish between wishes, dreams, intentions and properly structured goals
Apply at least two evidence-based goal-setting frameworks
Memorise the names of every author in the course
Identify the psychology behind achievement and why goals fail

explanation: The fourth objective is to build a personal goal architecture. Memorising author names is not an objective.

prompt: Objective two asks you to apply at least {{1}} evidence-based goal-setting frameworks to your personal life.
explanation: At least two frameworks, applied to your own life, not merely recognised.

prompt: Match each level of aspiration to the problem the lecture identifies with it.
explanation: Wish, Dream, Intention, Goal, in ascending order of structure.

prompt: Match each example from the slide to its level.

pairs.left: "I want to own a business someday"
"I plan to start saving this year"
"I will save 20,000 naira monthly for 6 months from Jan 1st"

explanation: These are the slide's own four examples, one per level.

prompt: The slide's example of a real goal is: "I will save {{1}} naira monthly for {{2}} months from Jan 1st."
explanation: 20,000 naira monthly for 6 months from January 1st. Note 500,000 belongs to the opening story, not here.

prompt: The key shift is to move from "I want" to "I {{1}}, by [date], measured by [{{2}}]."
explanation: I will, by [date], measured by [evidence]. The word evidence is what makes it checkable.

prompt: According to the lecture, most people live in the Wish and Dream layers because those layers feel purposeful without requiring anything of them.
explanation: That is the slide's own explanation for why people stay there.

prompt: The lecture defines a real goal as a declaration with:

options.text: Evidence: what will happen, when, and how you will know
Passion: how strongly you feel about it
Support: who will hold you to it
Ambition: how far beyond your reach it sits

explanation: A goal is a declaration with evidence: what, when, and how you will know.

prompt: Match each goal type to what it describes.
explanation: Outcome is the result, Process is the doing, Identity is the becoming.

prompt: Match each example to its goal type.

pairs.left: "I am the kind of person who shows up consistently"

explanation: These are the three examples used on the slide.

prompt: Why does the lecture call Outcome Goals "dangerous alone"?

options.text: They are entirely outside your daily control
They are impossible to measure
They take longer than a year to reach
They cannot be written down clearly

explanation: Motivating and useful for direction, but outside your daily control, so dangerous on their own.

prompt: Which goal type does the lecture call "the daily engine of achievement"?

options.text: Process Goals
Outcome Goals
Identity Goals
Stretch Goals

explanation: Process Goals are fully within your control and build directly toward outcomes.

prompt: When the goal becomes your {{1}}, behaviour follows without negotiation. The student who {{2}} disciplined outlasts the one who wants to be.
explanation: The student who IS disciplined outlasts the one who WANTS to be. That is the whole case for Identity Goals.

prompt: The lecture ranks the three goal types by lasting power, with Outcome Goals having the greatest lasting power.
explanation: They are ranked by lasting power with IDENTITY highest. Only Identity Goals actually change you.

prompt: A student writes: "I will study four hours every weekday." A mentor tells him to rewrite it as an Identity Goal. Which rewrite is correct?

options.text: "I am becoming the kind of person who studies without being told"
"I will study five hours every weekday"
"I want to graduate with a first class"
"I will study four hours every weekday for one semester"

explanation: Identity Goals use the form "I am becoming the kind of person who...". Graduating with a first class is an Outcome Goal, and the two study-hours answers stay Process Goals.

prompt: In the class exercise you rewrite your goal as an Identity Goal using the stem: "I am {{1}} the kind of person who..."
explanation: The exercise stem is "I am becoming the kind of person who...".

prompt: Which steps belong to the "What Type Is Your Goal?" exercise? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Write down one current goal you are actively pursuing or avoiding
Identify its type: Outcome, Process or Identity
Share it immediately with the whole class
Rewrite it as an Identity Goal and notice how the rewrite feels

explanation: The exercise is done individually in five minutes; there is no whole-class share step.

prompt: The goal-type exercise is timed at {{1}} minutes and is done individually.
explanation: Five minutes, individually. The 4-Layer Goal Stack exercise on Slide 20 is the eight-minute one.

prompt: Match each framework to the failure it exists to solve.

pairs.right: Goals that lack structure and emotional connection
Ambition with no measurable evidence of progress
Motivation without a trigger to act

explanation: Each of the four frameworks answers a different failure mode. This pairing is high-yield.

prompt: How does the lecture tell you to use the four frameworks?

options.text: As a toolkit, not as a menu to pick one from
As a menu, choosing whichever suits you
In strict order, one per year
Only after you have failed at least once

explanation: A toolkit, not a menu. You are meant to use them together.

prompt: Framework 3 is the {{1}}-Week Year, and framework 4 is Implementation {{2}}.
explanation: The order is SMART+ER, OKRs, 12-Week Year, Implementation Intentions.

prompt: Match each SMART letter to its question.

pairs.right: Exactly what will you do or produce?
Is this a genuine but realistic stretch?

extraLabels: Does this serve your bigger purpose?
When exactly will you check progress?
explanation: S Specific, M Measurable, A Achievable, T Time-bound. The two decoys are R Relevant and +R Reviewed.

prompt: The two letters SMART+ER adds are {{1}}, meaning would you pursue this without anyone watching, and {{2}}, meaning when exactly will you check progress.
explanation: +E Exciting and +R Reviewed. Relevant is the plain SMART R and is a deliberate trap.

prompt: What does the lecture call the fatal weakness of plain SMART?

options.text: A SMART goal can be abandoned by week 2 because it has no emotional connection
SMART goals are always too easy
SMART goals cannot be measured objectively
SMART goals take too long to write

explanation: No emotional connection, so it can be abandoned by week 2. E supplies internal fuel and R supplies accountability.

prompt: A goal without a review schedule is a {{1}} with an expiry date.
explanation: A wish with an expiry date. It links straight back to the four levels on Slide 4.

prompt: Which statements about the two added letters are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: E stands for Exciting and supplies internal fuel
R stands for Reviewed and builds in accountability
E stands for Easy, so the goal needs no effort
R stands for Relevant, which is the same R already in SMART

explanation: Exciting and Reviewed. The Relevant answer confuses the added R with the existing SMART R.

prompt: OKRs have been used by {{1}} since {{2}}.
explanation: Google since 1999. The slide's subtitle is "Ambition Meets Evidence".

prompt: An OKR is made of which two parts?

options.text: One qualitative Objective plus 2 to 4 measurable Key Results
A wish and a deadline
A vision and a weekly scorecard
A list of daily activities and a review date

explanation: One bold qualitative Objective, and 2 to 4 Key Results that prove it.

prompt: Match each OKR part to the question it answers.

pairs.right: How will I know I got there?

explanation: The Objective sets direction; the Key Results supply evidence.

prompt: Which of these is a Key Result rather than an activity?

options.text: Secure 3 mentors by end of quarter
Attend networking events
Read about the industry regularly
Try to meet more senior people

explanation: Activities describe what you do; Key Results describe what changes. "Attend networking events" is the slide's own example of the wrong answer.

prompt: Activities describe what you {{1}}. Key Results describe what {{2}}.
explanation: That one-line distinction is the most tested idea in the OKR section.

prompt: An OKR should carry between 2 and 4 Key Results.
explanation: Two to four measurable Key Results per Objective.

prompt: How ambitious should the Objective be?

options.text: Ambitious enough to feel slightly uncomfortable
Comfortable enough to guarantee success
Impossible, so you always have room to grow
Identical to last quarter's, for consistency

explanation: One bold, inspiring, qualitative statement, ambitious enough to feel slightly uncomfortable.

prompt: Adaeze is a {{1}}-Level Mass Communication student. Her end-of-quarter OKR score was {{2}}, rated Strong.
explanation: 300-Level Mass Comm, overall 0.76 (Strong). Do not confuse 0.76 overall with the 0.75 posts KR.

prompt: Match each of Adaeze's Key Results to the score it earned.
explanation: 0.75, 1.0, 0.5 and 0.8, giving a weighted overall of 0.76. The 0.76 label is the decoy.

prompt: Adaeze's first Key Result was to publish {{1}} posts of at least {{2}} views each by April 30. She published {{3}}.
explanation: 12 posts at minimum 200 views by 30 April; 9 published, so 9 of 12 = 0.75.

prompt: Her LinkedIn Key Result was to grow to {{1}} connections at {{2}} engagement by May 31. She reached {{3}}.
explanation: 500 connections at 3% engagement; she reached 412, scoring 0.8.

prompt: What does the lecture say OKR scoring replaces?

options.text: Vague guilt, with a structured conversation about what changes next quarter
Annual appraisals, with weekly check-ins
Self-discipline, with external supervision
Long-term vision, with short-term targets

explanation: Scoring replaces vague guilt with a structured conversation about what changes next quarter.

prompt: Adaeze reviews her quarter. Her Objective was {{1}} Her scores show a mixed but strong quarter, because {{2}} The overall figure of 0.76 matters because {{3}}

accept: to establish herself as a credible emerging voice in digital media before the end of the academic year
choices: to establish herself as a credible emerging voice in digital media before the end of the academic year
to graduate with a first class degree in Mass Communication
to secure a paid internship at a national newspaper

accept: some Key Results were fully met, like the internship at 1.0, while others fell short, like mentors at 0.5
choices: some Key Results were fully met, like the internship at 1.0, while others fell short, like mentors at 0.5
every Key Result was met in full and the quarter was a complete success
none of the Key Results were met, so the objective failed

accept: it reflects weighted performance across all Key Results and shows substantial progress even where full achievement was not reached
choices: it reflects weighted performance across all Key Results and shows substantial progress even where full achievement was not reached
it is the average of the two highest scoring Key Results only
it is the score of the single most important Key Result

explanation: The Objective was to be a credible emerging voice in digital media; 0.76 is a weighted score across all KRs, showing real progress without full achievement.

prompt: Her mentors Key Result asked for {{1}} active industry mentors with one conversation per month by March {{2}}.
explanation: 2 active mentors, 1 conversation a month, by 31 March. She found 1, scoring 0.5.

prompt: Match each element of a 12-Week cycle to its description.

pairs.right: Your long-term why that does not change weekly
One to three specific goals for this cycle only
Specific scheduled actions, written not mental
Percentage of planned actions completed, target 85% or more

explanation: The fifth element, Weekly Review, asks what worked and what changes next week.

prompt: The Weekly Scorecard target is {{1}} or more of planned actions completed. The framework is credited to Brian {{2}}.
explanation: 85% or more, Brian Moran's solution: treat every 12 weeks as a full year.

prompt: With 12 months to achieve a goal the brain behaves as though there is always more time: urgency is low in {{1}}, relevance fades in {{2}}, and panic arrives in {{3}}, too late for a full recovery.
explanation: Low in January, fading by June, panic in October. This is the argument for short cycles.

prompt: How many fresh starts a year does the 12-Week Year create?

options.text: Four
Twelve
Two
One

explanation: Execution is compressed into 12-week cycles, giving four fresh starts a year.

prompt: In the 12-Week Year the Weekly Plan may be held mentally rather than written down.
explanation: The slide is explicit: written, not mental.

prompt: Which are among the five elements of a 12-Week cycle? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Vision
Weekly Scorecard
Annual Budget
Weekly Review

explanation: Vision, 12-Week Goal, Weekly Plan, Weekly Scorecard, Weekly Review. There is no budget element.

prompt: Psychologist Peter {{1}} found a follow-through rate of {{2}} among people who specified exactly when and where they would act, against {{3}} for those with intention only.
explanation: Gollwitzer, 71% against 32%. These two figures are among the most tested numbers in the course.

prompt: The Implementation Intention formula is: "When [specific {{1}}] occurs, I will [specific {{2}}]."
explanation: When [specific cue] occurs, I will [specific behaviour].

prompt: Which of these is a properly formed cue?

options.text: When I sit down at my desk on Monday at 6 PM
When I feel motivated
When I am no longer stressed
When I finally feel ready

explanation: The cue must be concrete: a time, a place, or a completed action. Emotional cues are exactly what the slide forbids.

prompt: What can serve as a concrete cue? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A time
A place
A feeling of readiness
A completed action

explanation: Time, place or completed action. Never a feeling.

prompt: Gollwitzer found that specifying when and where roughly two to three times more people followed through.
explanation: Two to three times more often, the concrete figures being 71% against 32%.

prompt: The purpose of an Implementation Intention is to pre-decide, so that your {{1}} self does not negotiate.
explanation: Pre-decide so your future self does not negotiate.

prompt: Match each step of the six-step method to what it asks.

pairs.right: Name the goal behaviour: one specific action
Chain it to an existing habit

explanation: The two decoys are steps 3 and 5, which are real steps in the wrong slots.

prompt: The method has {{1}} steps. Step 5 pre-empts the obstacle with the form: "If [temptation], then I will [{{2}}]."
explanation: Six steps, and step 5 is the if-then counter-action.

prompt: Which are among the six steps for using Implementation Intentions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Find a reliable daily cue: time, place or existing routine
Chain it to an existing habit for automatic triggering
Tell at least three people about the goal
Identify your failure mode, when and why it typically does not happen

explanation: Telling three people belongs to Lecture Three's self-audit, not to this six-step method.

prompt: The Implementation Intention exercise takes {{1}} minutes and ends by connecting the new behaviour to an existing habit with the stem: "After I [habit], I will [{{2}}]."
explanation: Five minutes, ending with habit chaining.

prompt: Which questions does the "Build One Implementation Intention" exercise ask? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: What is the specific behaviour the goal requires, one concrete action?
What is your most predictable failure mode?
How much money will the goal require?
Write your Obstacle Plan: "If ___ happens, then I will ___"

explanation: Cost is never part of this exercise.

prompt: Match each reason goals fail to its fix.

pairs.right: Add a 40% time buffer and work backwards from the deadline
Design your system for the middle, not the launch
Design your environment so the right behaviour needs least resistance

explanation: Three reasons, three fixes, and the lecture insists none of them is laziness.

prompt: The Planning Fallacy is answered by adding a {{1}} time buffer. Motivation Decay bites hardest in weeks {{2}} to {{3}}.
explanation: 40% buffer; weeks 3 to 8 are the dangerous middle where most people quit.

prompt: The lecture gives three reasons goals fail, and none of them is laziness.
explanation: That is the slide's own subtitle: "None of Them Is Laziness".

prompt: How does the lecture describe the Planning Fallacy?

options.text: We overestimate what we can do short-term and underestimate long-term capacity
We plan too much and act too little
We copy other people's plans instead of writing our own
We plan only when motivated

explanation: Short-term overestimate, long-term underestimate. The fix is the 40% buffer.

prompt: A student is in week 5 of a 12-week goal and has lost all enthusiasm. Which failure does the lecture name, and what is its fix?

options.text: Motivation Decay; design the system for the middle rather than the launch
Planning Fallacy; add a 40% time buffer
Willpower Depletion; rely on discipline until it passes
Wrong goal type; switch to an Outcome Goal

explanation: Week 5 sits inside the dangerous middle of weeks 3 to 8. The fix is designing for the middle.

prompt: Willpower Depletion means self-control tires with use, so relying on willpower alone is a {{1}} strategy.
explanation: A losing strategy; design the environment instead.

prompt: Match each achievement strategy to its description.

pairs.right: Attach a new goal behaviour to an existing daily habit
Pair a hard task with something you enjoy
Commit to just 2 minutes; the goal is to start, not to finish
Small wins are the biggest driver of motivation

explanation: The six strategies are Habit Stacking, Temptation Bundling, the 2-Minute Rule, the Progress Principle, Accountability and WOOP.

prompt: Temptation bundling raised exercise by {{1}} when paired with audiobooks. A structured accountability partner raises goal completion to {{2}}. The Progress Principle comes from Harvard research by {{3}}.
explanation: +51% exercise, 95% completion with an accountability partner (ASTD), and Amabile at Harvard for the Progress Principle.

prompt: What is the point of the 2-Minute Rule?

options.text: The goal is to start, not to finish
Every task should be completed within two minutes
You should rest for two minutes between tasks
Two minutes of planning saves an hour of work

explanation: Commit to just two minutes of a hard task. Starting is the whole objective.

prompt: The slide sets the six strategies under which heading?

options.text: Environment and Systems, not Willpower and Inspiration
Discipline and Sacrifice, not Comfort
Talent and Opportunity, not Effort
Vision and Faith, not Planning

explanation: Environment and Systems, not Willpower and Inspiration. It follows directly from Willpower Depletion.

prompt: Which are among the six achievement strategies? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Habit Stacking
WOOP
Visualisation alone
The Progress Principle

explanation: Visualisation alone is precisely what WOOP's mental contrasting is said to outperform.

prompt: For the Progress Principle the lecture recommends keeping a daily progress {{1}}.
explanation: A daily progress journal, because small wins are the biggest driver of motivation.

prompt: The 95% figure in Lecture One refers to people who write their goals down and share them with an accountability partner.
explanation: Lecture One's 95% is goal completion with a structured accountability partner. The write-and-share figure is 76%, and it belongs to Lecture Five.

prompt: Match each WOOP letter to its step.

pairs.right: Wish: state your most important goal clearly
Outcome: visualise the best possible result vividly
Obstacle: name the biggest internal obstacle honestly

explanation: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan.

prompt: What does the lecture say mental contrasting outperforms?

options.text: Positive visualisation
Habit stacking
Accountability partnerships
Written goal setting

explanation: Mental contrasting outperforms positive visualisation. Imagining the win alone is not enough.

prompt: In WOOP the obstacle you name must be the biggest {{1}} obstacle, answered honestly.
explanation: Internal, not external. What has stopped you before.

prompt: The slide's worked example runs as follows. The Wish is {{1}} The Obstacle is {{2}} and the Plan is {{3}}

accept: to finish my research proposal this month
choices: to finish my research proposal this month
to graduate with a first class degree this year
to secure two mentors this quarter

accept: being distracted by social media when working alone
choices: being distracted by social media when working alone
not having enough time in the day
a supervisor who is difficult to reach

accept: when I sit to write, I switch my phone to airplane mode first
choices: when I sit to write, I switch my phone to airplane mode first
I will ask a friend to check on me every evening
I will work in the library instead of my room

explanation: Wish: finish the research proposal this month. Obstacle: social media when working alone. Plan: airplane mode before writing.

prompt: In the WOOP example, the Outcome step says the supervisor {{1}} it and you feel proud and ahead of schedule.
explanation: Outcome: the supervisor approves it; you feel proud and ahead of schedule.

prompt: Which are dimensions of the Total Man framework? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Spiritual
Financial
Political
Physical

explanation: The five are Spiritual, Mental, Physical, Social and Financial. There is no political dimension.

prompt: Match each Total Man dimension to what it covers.
explanation: The decoy "stewardship and wealth-building" is the Financial dimension.

prompt: The Total Man framework has {{1}} dimensions, and the slide's heading warns that winning in one area while {{2}} in another is not success.
explanation: Five dimensions, and whole-life excellence is the point.

prompt: Which are the three questions for aligned goal setting? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Does this goal serve my purpose, not just my preference?
Am I building in every dimension, or winning in one while crumbling in others?
Will this goal impress the people around me?
Is this goal aligned with who God has called me to be?

explanation: Purpose not preference; every dimension; alignment with calling.

prompt: Match each layer of the Goal Stack to its timeframe.
explanation: 10 to 20 years, 1 to 3 years, 12 weeks, 7 days.

prompt: Match each layer to the question it asks.

pairs.right: Who am I called to be?
What must I build toward that vision?
What do I commit to right now?
What do I actually do this week?

extraLabels: Who will hold me to it?
explanation: Each layer feeds the one above it.

prompt: In the 200-Level student example, the Quarterly target is to raise CGPA by {{1}} points this semester, and the Weekly action is notes done Friday and study group Saturday at {{2}}.
explanation: Raise CGPA 0.2 points; notes Friday, study group Saturday 10am.

prompt: In the same example, the Life Vision is to lead political reform in {{1}} Africa, and the Strategic goal is a first class plus an MPA or LAW scholarship by {{2}}.
explanation: Lead political reform in West Africa; first class plus MPA or LAW scholarship by 2030.

prompt: The lecture says weekly actions are essentially random, and the vision is what matters.
explanation: The opposite: weekly actions are not random, they are the bricks that build the vision.

prompt: Which instructions belong to the "Build Your 4-Layer Goal Stack" exercise? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Write your Life Vision in two sentences, a person description, not a job title
Write one concrete weekly action with day, time and location
Read your full stack aloud to the class
Pair share: read only your Weekly Action to the person beside you and exchange contacts

explanation: You read only the Weekly Action, and only to the person beside you.

prompt: The Goal Stack exercise takes {{1}} minutes and is worked {{2}}-down.
explanation: Eight minutes, top-down from Life Vision to Weekly Action.

prompt: The exercise says your Life Vision should be written as:

options.text: Two sentences describing a person, not a job title
A single job title you are aiming for
A list of five achievements
One sentence naming your salary target

explanation: Not a job title, but a person description in two sentences.

prompt: A student says "I want to be successful." The lecture would classify this as {{1}} To fix it he must {{2}} and the most durable rewrite of all would be {{3}}

accept: a wish, because it has no direction and no deadline
choices: a wish, because it has no direction and no deadline
a dream, because the timeframe is indefinite
an intention, because he has committed to it

accept: move from "I want" to "I will, by [date], measured by [evidence]"
choices: move from "I want" to "I will, by [date], measured by [evidence]"
simply want it more strongly and repeat it daily
wait until he feels motivated enough to begin

accept: an Identity Goal, because when the goal becomes who you are, behaviour follows without negotiation
choices: an Identity Goal, because when the goal becomes who you are, behaviour follows without negotiation
an Outcome Goal, because outcomes are the most motivating
a Process Goal, because process is the only thing that lasts

explanation: Wish is the lowest level; the fix is the I will formula; Identity Goals have the greatest lasting power.

prompt: A student drafts an OKR whose Key Results read "attend networking events" and "read more industry blogs". The lecture's objection is {{1}} A correct rewrite would be {{2}} And once the quarter ends, scoring matters because {{3}}

accept: these are activities, not Key Results, because they describe what he does rather than what changes
choices: these are activities, not Key Results, because they describe what he does rather than what changes
there are only two of them, and an OKR needs at least five
they are too ambitious to be achievable within one quarter

accept: "secure 3 mentors by end of quarter", which states a measurable outcome
choices: "secure 3 mentors by end of quarter", which states a measurable outcome
"attend one networking event every week without fail"
"spend two hours a day reading industry blogs"

accept: it replaces vague guilt with a structured conversation about what changes next quarter
choices: it replaces vague guilt with a structured conversation about what changes next quarter
it decides whether the objective should be abandoned entirely
it determines how much time to allocate next year

explanation: Activities describe what you do; Key Results describe what changes. Scoring exists to structure the next quarter.

prompt: A student sets a twelve-month goal in January and has done nothing by June. The 12-Week Year diagnoses this as {{1}} The psychology section adds that {{2}} The practical fix is {{3}}

accept: annual timelines letting the brain behave as though there is always more time, so urgency is low in January and relevance fades by June
choices: annual timelines letting the brain behave as though there is always more time, so urgency is low in January and relevance fades by June
a goal that was never specific enough to act on in the first place
a lack of natural talent for the subject

accept: motivation peaks at the start and end, and weeks 3 to 8 are the dangerous middle where most people quit
choices: motivation peaks at the start and end, and weeks 3 to 8 are the dangerous middle where most people quit
motivation is constant, so the failure must be laziness
motivation only matters in the final month before the deadline

accept: compress execution into 12-week cycles and track a weekly scorecard against an 85% target
choices: compress execution into 12-week cycles and track a weekly scorecard against an 85% target
extend the deadline by another twelve months to reduce pressure
abandon the goal and choose an easier one

explanation: January to June is exactly the decay the 12-Week Year is built to defeat, with 85% as the weekly scorecard target.

prompt: A student writes "When I feel stressed, I will revise." The lecture rejects this because {{1}} A correct version would be {{2}} He could strengthen it further by {{3}}

accept: the cue is emotional and vague, and a cue must be concrete: a time, a place or a completed action
choices: the cue is emotional and vague, and a cue must be concrete: a time, a place or a completed action
the behaviour is too small to be worth pre-deciding
stress is not a real obstacle to revision

accept: "When I sit down at my desk on Monday at 6 PM, I will complete my weekly planning worksheet"
choices: "When I sit down at my desk on Monday at 6 PM, I will complete my weekly planning worksheet"
"When I have the energy, I will revise for as long as I can"
"When my friends are also studying, I will join them"

accept: habit stacking, chaining the new behaviour to an existing daily habit so it triggers automatically
choices: habit stacking, chaining the new behaviour to an existing daily habit so it triggers automatically
relying on willpower, which strengthens the more it is used
waiting for motivation to return naturally

explanation: Emotional cues are the classic error; 71% against 32% is the payoff for getting the cue concrete.

prompt: The 95% accountability figure is attributed to {{1}}.
explanation: The American Society for Training and Development, cited on the slide as ASTD.

prompt: A student pairs his least favourite module with the podcast he loves, and only listens while studying it. Which strategy is this?

options.text: Temptation Bundling
Habit Stacking
The 2-Minute Rule
The Progress Principle

explanation: Pairing a hard task with something enjoyable is temptation bundling, worth +51% in the cited research.

prompt: Which statements correctly pair a framework with its detail? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: SMART+ER adds Exciting and Reviewed to the five SMART letters
OKRs have been used by Google since 1999
The 12-Week Year was developed by Peter Gollwitzer
Implementation Intentions solve motivation without a trigger to act

explanation: The 12-Week Year is Brian Moran's. Gollwitzer is Implementation Intentions.

prompt: Where in the 4-Layer Goal Stack does an Identity Goal most naturally sit?

options.text: Life Vision, because it answers who you are called to be
Weekly Actions, because identity is built daily
Quarterly Targets, because a quarter is long enough to change
Strategic Goals, because identity takes one to three years

explanation: The Life Vision layer's own question is "Who am I called to be?", which is the Identity Goal question.

prompt: In SMART, {{1}} asks what number proves you succeeded, and {{2}} asks whether this serves your bigger purpose.
explanation: M Measurable and R Relevant. Reviewed is the added +R.

prompt: In the opening story, the first roommate wrote "I want to be successful".
explanation: That single sentence, unchanged four years later, is the whole point of the story.

prompt: Which verb does the fourth learning objective use?

options.text: Build a personal goal architecture using proven modern strategies
Evaluate the frameworks against each other
